lessons.title: Monetary Policy Refresher: How the RBI's MPC Sets the Tone

body.text: If the Union Budget tells you how the government plans to spend and borrow, the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee tells you what money itself will cost for the next two months, and in a leveraged economy, that number touches everything from your home loan EMI to the price the market pays for a stock's future earnings.

markDefs.definition: The interest rate at which the RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks against government securities collateral. It is the RBI's primary tool for signalling the direction of borrowing costs across the economy.

children.text: The Monetary Policy Committee, or MPC, is a six-member panel, three from the Reserve Bank of India and three external members appointed by the government, that meets six times a year to decide the

, the interest rate at which the RBI lends short-term money to commercial banks. Since 2016, the MPC has operated under a legislated mandate: keep retail inflation, measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI), at 4%, with a tolerance band of plus or minus 2 percentage points.

That mandate matters more than it sounds. It means the MPC is not free to chase growth at any cost, and it is not free to fight inflation at any cost either. Every rate decision is a judgment call on where India sits inside that four-plus-or-minus-two band, and how much risk the committee is willing to take with growth to get inflation back inside it.

body.label: RBI's inflation target
body.context: Legislated under the RBI Act amendment of 2016. If inflation stays outside this band for three straight quarters, the MPC is required to send the government a written explanation and a plan to bring it back.

children.text: How a Repo Rate Cut Actually Reaches Your Portfolio

markDefs.definition: External Benchmark Lending Rate: since 2019, banks must price most floating-rate retail and small business loans off an external benchmark, usually the repo rate, rather than their own internal cost-of-funds calculation. This was designed specifically to make rate cuts and hikes reach borrowers faster.

children.text: A repo rate cut does not move through the economy instantly, and it does not move through every loan at the same speed. Loans priced off the
External Benchmark Lending Rate, or EBLR

, such as most new floating-rate home loans, reprice within a quarter of a rate change because banks are required to reset them at fixed intervals. Older loans still linked to a bank's internal MCLR, or Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate, take longer to adjust because MCLR itself only moves as a bank's own cost of deposits changes.

This is also why bank stocks do not all react the same way to a rate cut. A bank with a large book of EBLR-linked loans sees its lending yield fall almost immediately, while its deposit costs take longer to reprice downward, which can squeeze net interest margin, or NIM, in the short run even though the cut is broadly positive for credit growth over time.

body.text: Notice the shape of this cycle: a sharp Covid-era cut, a long hold near the bottom, a fast hiking cycle once inflation broke above the tolerance band, an extended hold near the peak, and then cuts only once the MPC was convinced inflation had genuinely cooled. Holds are policy decisions too, not the absence of one.

body.title: Same Cut, Different Bank
body.scenario: The MPC cuts the repo rate by 25 basis points. Bank A has 70% of its loan book linked to EBLR and reprices most of it within weeks. Bank B has 60% of its loan book still on older MCLR-linked contracts that reprice gradually over the next several quarters.
body.prompt: In the quarter immediately after the cut, which bank is more likely to see near-term margin pressure, and why might the market still prefer holding that bank into a rate-cut cycle?
body.modelAnswer: Bank A, with more EBLR-linked loans, reprices its lending yield down faster than it can reprice deposit costs, so its net interest margin typically compresses first and fastest in the near term. Bank B's margin holds up better in the short run simply because its book is slower to reprice. Even so, the market often prefers banks like Bank A heading into a sustained cutting cycle, because faster repricing also means faster credit growth as EMIs fall and loan demand picks up, and the margin pressure is usually a one-to-two-quarter phenomenon rather than a permanent impairment.

children.text: The MPC's Toolkit Beyond the Repo Rate
The repo rate gets the headlines, but the RBI manages the money market between MPC meetings using tools that never require a formal rate decision.

cells: Sets the benchmark cost of short-term borrowing for banks
Changed only at scheduled MPC meetings
Share of deposits banks must park with the RBI, earning no interest
Tightens or loosens systemic liquidity directly, independent of the rate itself
RBI buys or sells G-Secs in the secondary market
Manages day-to-day banking system liquidity and can cap bond yields between meetings
Forward guidance: accommodative, neutral, or withdrawal of accommodation
Signals the likely direction of future rate moves without changing the rate itself

body.title: Accommodative Stance vs Withdrawal of Accommodation

columns.label: Accommodative Stance
points: Signals the MPC is willing to cut rates further, or at minimum will not hike
Usually paired with ample banking system liquidity
Read as supportive for equities and for rate-sensitive sectors like autos, real estate and banks

columns.label: Withdrawal of Accommodation
points: Signals the MPC is done easing and is watching for the right moment to tighten or hold firm
Often paired with active liquidity draining through OMO sales or CRR hikes
Read cautiously by bond markets even if the repo rate itself does not move that meeting

children.text: Reading an MPC Statement Like a Professional

The rate decision itself is often the least interesting part of the statement for a professional. What moves Nifty and Bank Nifty on MPC day is usually the vote split (a unanimous decision reads very differently from a 4-2 split), the exact wording of the stance, and the Governor's tone in the press conference that follows. A repo rate cut delivered alongside a stance that stays at withdrawal of accommodation, sometimes called a hawkish cut, tells the market this is a one-off adjustment, not the start of a cutting cycle, and bond yields can actually rise on a day the RBI cut rates.

body.title: Your MPC Day Checklist
steps: Check the rate decision itself, but do not stop there
Check the vote split: unanimous versus a narrow majority signals very different conviction within the committee
Read the exact stance language, since a stance change often matters more to markets than the rate move itself
Listen to the Governor's press conference for inflation and growth projections, not just the headline number
Watch the 10-year G-Sec yield in the minutes after the statement, since bond markets often move opposite to what the headline rate action suggests if the stance surprises

body.title: The Hawkish Cut
body.question: The MPC cuts the repo rate by 25 basis points, but keeps its stance at withdrawal of accommodation and flags that inflation risks remain to the upside. What is the most likely bond market reaction, and why?
options: 10-year G-Sec yields fall sharply, since any rate cut is unambiguously bond-positive regardless of stance
10-year G-Sec yields may rise or stay flat, because the stance and inflation commentary signal this cut is unlikely to be the start of a sustained easing cycle
Bond yields are unaffected by MPC stance language and only react to the repo rate number itself
This combination is not possible, since a rate cut and a hawkish stance never occur in the same statement
body.explanation: Bond markets price in an expected path of future rate cuts, not just the one just delivered. If the stance stays hawkish (withdrawal of accommodation) and the MPC flags upside inflation risk, the market reads this as a cautious, possibly one-off cut rather than the start of a sustained cycle, which can leave the 10-year G-Sec yield flat or even push it higher if the market had been pricing in faster or deeper cuts ahead.

body.title: Real Interest Rate Check
body.prompt: The repo rate is 6.50% and CPI inflation is running at 5.00%. What is the approximate real interest rate, in percentage points?
body.explanation: The real interest rate is a simple approximation: the nominal repo rate minus the current inflation rate. Here, 6.50% minus 5.00% equals 1.50%. A low or negative real rate generally signals an accommodative policy environment, supportive for growth assets, while a high positive real rate signals a restrictive environment aimed at cooling demand.

body.label: RBI Monetary Policy Statements (official)
body.description: The full MPC resolution, statement and minutes, including the individual vote and reasoning of each committee member, published a few weeks after every meeting.

body.text: Nothing in this lesson is investment advice. It is educational content on how monetary policy mechanics tend to move markets, consistent with SEBI's guidelines for registered research analysts on this platform.

points: The MPC's legal mandate is 4% CPI inflation with a plus or minus 2 percentage point band, not growth maximisation in isolation
How fast a rate change reaches you depends on whether your loan is linked to EBLR or the older MCLR, and the same is true of how fast it reaches a bank's margins
CRR, OMOs and policy stance let the RBI manage liquidity and signal intent between MPC meetings, without touching the repo rate itself
The vote split and stance language on MPC day often matter more to markets than the headline rate decision
A rate cut paired with a hawkish stance (a hawkish cut) can leave bond yields flat or higher, because markets price the expected path of future policy, not just the single decision just made
